title_patterns: [TICKER] earnings: the [specific metric] nobody is checking — with the actual number
[NAMED ANALYST/SOURCE]: [specific price target] and [specific % move] — what the math assumes
I backtested [well-known group / claim] — here's the [specific return figure]
[ASSET/YIELD] just hit [unrounded level], the highest since [specific year/event] — what that historically implied
[MACRO EVENT] moved [specific instrument] by [exact bps/%] — three second-order effects
Post-[EARNINGS EVENT]: which [N] suppliers actually saw revenue change (data, not reaction)
[COMPANY]'s first earnings report as a public company: [N] numbers that matter
[SECTOR] insiders bought $[exact amount] of their own stock — the full filing breakdown
hook_patterns: Open with the single hardest number from the report and state exactly what it changed — no preamble.
State the widely repeated claim in one sentence, then say 'here's what the data actually shows' and go straight to the figure.
Timestamp the setup: 'As of [date], [metric] sits at [exact level]. Last time it did, here's what followed.'
Name the three numbers the video will cover in the first 15 seconds, so viewers know the payoff structure.
Lead with what you were wrong about or what the consensus missed, then quantify the gap.
packaging_notes: Two clear duration pockets: 5–9 min single-catalyst explainers (earnings, one macro print, one datapoint) and 17–25 min multi-stock or backtest deep dives. Avoid the 10–15 min middle unless it's a genuine roundup.

Unrounded, verifiable numbers in the title outperform adjectives — a price target, a bps move, a dollar filing amount, or a year reference ('highest since ___') does the work that hype words usually attempt.
Earnings-reaction videos published within 24–48 hours of the print get outsized lift; second-order framing ('who benefits downstream') beats 'good or bad quarter'.
Attribution framing (named analyst, named filing, named agency) borrows credibility without emotion — use the source as the hook instead of a threat.
'I tested / I backtested / I checked the filings' first-person research framing is the cleanest way to make a skeptical, data-first angle feel like a story.
Skip collapse/implosion language and alarm emojis; substitute a specific mechanism ('30-year yields at X% raise refi costs by Y') which conveys stakes while staying inside the no-hype positioning.
market_patterns.title: outlier pattern extraction

winning_patterns.pattern: Named human or named institution as the acting subject, followed by a behavioral anomaly (acted repeatedly, acted late, acted against the obvious incentive).
winning_patterns.evidence: Our two strongest retention videos both put a specific person at the center (a politician's delayed disclosure, an executive's repeated same-day selling): hook_hold 1.18 and 1.28, avg_view_pct 84% and 93%.
winning_patterns.why_it_works: A named actor gives the viewer someone to judge in the first 5 seconds; the anomaly creates an open question the video must answer, so they stay to see the resolution.

winning_patterns.pattern: Two-part title where the second clause undercuts or reframes the first (move happened, but the stated reason was not the real one).
winning_patterns.evidence: Titles built on 'the catalyst was pre-scheduled', 'priced in something not yet real', 'moved on a headline it didn't originate', 'rallied despite bad news' all cleared 68-88% avg_view_pct with hook_hold above 1.0.
winning_patterns.why_it_works: The qualifier promises analysis, not just a recap. It signals the video contains a mechanism the viewer doesn't already know.

winning_patterns.pattern: One precise number carrying the whole hook — exact digits or an oddly specific count, not a rounded headline figure.
winning_patterns.structure: [Exact figure] + [mechanical detail: number of trades, sessions, filings]
winning_patterns.evidence: An exact-dollar figure split across a stated trade count held 72% with hook_hold 1.13; a 'sold N times in one day' framing held 93%. Rounded big-dollar figures with no mechanism underperformed.
winning_patterns.why_it_works: Precision reads as primary-source data rather than commentary, which matches what this audience shows up for; the mechanical detail implies the video explains the how.

winning_patterns.pattern: Single-event, single-ticker, short-form scope: one anomaly per video, nothing bundled.
winning_patterns.structure: One subject, one number, one question
winning_patterns.evidence: Every video above 70% avg_view_pct is short-form and covers exactly one situation. Both multi-story videos sat at 29-35% avg_view_pct.
winning_patterns.why_it_works: Scope matches the promise, so there's no point where the viewer feels the specific thing they clicked for is already over.

losing_patterns.pattern: Dated market-recap titles with a colon, a date, and a stacked multi-clause headline.
losing_patterns.structure: [Show name]: [Date] — [Story A detail, Story B detail]
losing_patterns.evidence: Both titles in this shape are our two worst hook holds (0.50, 0.50) and bottom-tier retention (29-35%), despite being our longest videos.
losing_patterns.why_it_fails: The date front-loads the title with zero tension, and the stacked clauses tell the viewer the payoff is already delivered. Nothing is left unresolved.

losing_patterns.pattern: Bare ticker abbreviation as the opening token with no orienting context.
losing_patterns.evidence: Ticker-led titles were highly inconsistent, including two of our weakest holds (0.79-0.89) and sub-55% retention; the ticker-led entries that did work carried an unusually strong contradiction clause behind them.
losing_patterns.why_it_fails: An unrecognized ticker makes the viewer resolve 'what is this' before they can care, which spends the hook window on decoding instead of curiosity.

losing_patterns.pattern: Large rounded dollar figure attached to a low-familiarity entity, with no actor and no mechanism.
losing_patterns.evidence: A rounded nine-figure block-trade title fell to 48% avg_view_pct with hook_hold 0.93, while a comparable figure broken into exact digits plus a trade count held 72%.
losing_patterns.why_it_fails: Size alone isn't a question. Without a named actor or a stated oddity, the viewer assumes routine institutional flow.

losing_patterns.pattern: Near-duplicate coverage of the same situation across two uploads with only the number or phrasing changed.
losing_patterns.evidence: The repeated small-cap insider-buying story landed at 49% and 35% avg_view_pct on 17 and 14 views.
losing_patterns.why_it_fails: The second version competes with the first for the same narrow audience and offers no new unresolved question.

notes: Sample is thin — 20 videos, most under 100 views — so treat these as directional. The clearest, most repeated signal is duration and scope: both long multi-story videos underperformed every short single-story video on hook hold.

insider_watch is bimodal, not weak: it produced our best-retaining video (single named executive, repeated action) and several of our worst (rounded dollar blocks, ticker-only, duplicated stories). The franchise works when there's an identifiable person behaving strangely.
The congress-trade angle has only one data point but it's our top performer on views and near-top on retention. Worth testing 2-3 more before drawing conclusions.
